issue.title: `LazyFrame.unnest` followed by a struct field read of another column loses or swaps column values (main)

labels.name: repo-6716405b
labels.description: Issue introduced by a new release

issue.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

(Not in a release: 2.1.0 and 2.0.0 are correct. It is on main, 09251856d4.)

### Reproducible example

```python
import polars as pl

# 1. in-memory engine: column `a` is lost and `t` appears twice
lf = pl.LazyFrame({"s": [{"a": 1}], "t": [{"p": 2, "q": 3}]})
q = lf.unnest("s").with_columns(t=pl.col("t").struct.field("p"))
print(q.collect_schema().names())
# ['a', 't']
print(q.collect(engine="in-memory"))
# shape: (1, 2)
# ┌───────────┬─────┐
# │ t         ┆ t   │
# │ ---       ┆ --- │
# │ struct[2] ┆ i64 │
# ╞═══════════╪═════╡
# │ {2,3}     ┆ 2   │
# └───────────┴─────┘
print(q.collect().columns)  # streaming
# ['t', 'a']

# 2. streaming engine: two joins after the unnest swap the values of `a` and `b`
lf = pl.LazyFrame({"k": [1], "s": [{"a": {"p": 1, "q": 2}}], "b": [{"p": 100, "q": 200}]})
other = pl.LazyFrame({"k": [1]})
q = lf.unnest("s").join(other, on="k").join(other, on="k").select("a", pl.col("b").struct.field("p"))
print(q.collect().to_dict(as_series=False))
# {'a': [{'p': 100, 'q': 200}], 'p': [1]}
# expected {'a': [{'p': 1, 'q': 2}], 'p': [100]}
```

### Log output

Plan of the first query on main; the scan is projected to `["t", "s"]`, so the unnest returns `[t, a]` while the schema above it is `[a, t]`:

```shell
 WITH_COLUMNS:
 [col("t").struct.field_by_name(p)().alias("t")]
  UNNEST by:[s]
    DF ["s", "t"]; PROJECT["t", "s"] 2/2 COLUMNS
```

On 2.1.0 the last line is `DF ["s", "t"]; PROJECT */2 COLUMNS`.

### Issue description

After `LazyFrame.unnest`, a query that needs every column but reads another struct column only in part (`struct.field`, and also `is_null()` on a struct or `list.len()` on a list of structs) gets the unnest output in a different column order than the plan's schema. Nothing puts the order back, and what happens next depends on the engine:

- **In-memory:** `with_columns` writes the new column at its schema position, over another column. In the example `a` is gone, `t` is there twice and `out["t"]` is the old struct. A following `.sort("a")` raises `ColumnNotFoundError`; with one more field in `s`, a self-join of the result panics with `duplicate name when building schema 't'` (`polars-core/src/frame/dataframe.rs`).
- **Streaming:** the values are right per name, but the column order of the result is not that of `collect_schema()`.
- **Streaming with two joins above the unnest:** two columns swap their values without an error (second example). The swap needs both columns to have the same dtype. With different dtypes it panics instead (`Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value in `polars-arrow/src/array/builder.rs`, or "The children must have the given number of values") or raises `ColumnNotFoundError` / `SchemaError: column name mismatch`.

It reproduces on `DataFrame.lazy()`, `scan_parquet`, `scan_ipc` and `scan_ndjson`, at 1, 2 and 8 threads. The eager `df.unnest(...)` and `QueryOptFlags(projection_pushdown=False)` give the right answer. Replacing `unnest` with 43 other operators (explode, joins, group_by, concat, unpivot, row index, ...) did not reproduce it.

This looks like the `FunctionIR::Unnest` arm in `projection_pushdown/mod.rs`. It pushes the pass-through columns first and the unnested struct last. Before #30598, a projection of every column in schema order was "no projection", so nothing was pushed below the unnest. With field pruning, a partial read of one column makes it a real projection. Its names are in schema order, so no reordering `simple π` is attached above the unnest, but the unnest output no longer has that order.

### Expected behavior

The first query returns columns `[a, t]` with values `[1]` and `[2]` on both engines. The second returns `{'a': [{'p': 1, 'q': 2}], 'p': [100]}`.

### Installed versions

Reproduces on main (09251856d4); 2.0.0 and 2.1.0 are correct. Regression from #30598 (3dae360c56).

issue.title: perf: Optimise decoding of Parquet `String` and `Binary` columns
issue.body:
Following on from the nested dtype optimisations in #30601, more profiling of flat/scalar Parquet reads showed decoding overhead for `String` and `Binary`, _especially_ for the `DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY` encoding[^1].

**Spoiler:** `DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY` encoding goes from ~5x slower than `pyarrow` to 1.1 → 2x faster. 🎉

# Changes

Both delta decoders were moved out of the `BinViewDecoder` match arms into a new `binview/delta.rs` module to consolidate/clarify, and `delta_byte_array::Decoder` drops the now-unused per-value iterator (dead code).

* **`PLAIN`**: short values (≤12 bytes, stored inline in the view) are now cut from a 16-byte block of the page instead of being copied one at a time.

* **`DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY`**: each page is decoded into views in bulk (all lengths at once,  one buffer, one UTF8 check per page); nulls and filters then reuse the existing PLAIN primitive kernels.

* ⭐ **`DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY`**: was allocating three `Vecs` per value and decoding the prefix/suffix lengths one at a time. Lengths are now decoded in bulk, and values are rebuilt in a single scratch buffer with fixed-size block copies.

**Also:**
* Delta-encoded pages with corrupt lengths now raise a `ComputeError` instead of panicking.
* Streamlined the `new_inline_from_block` function.

# Speedups 🚀

Testing on 20M rows[^2], `pyarrow`-written parquet, release build, single-column reads vs `main`.
Measured end-to-end with zstd (default threads) and uncompressed (single thread)[^3]:

### This PR vs `main`

| type/encoding | data | zstd | uncompressed |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| `String`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes            | 1.11x | 1.44x |
| `String`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes, 10% nulls | 1.14x | 1.47x |
| `Binary`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes            | 1.11x | 1.49x |
| `String`: DELTA_LENGTH     | 2-10 bytes            | 1.37x | 1.86x |
| `String`: DELTA_LENGTH     | 4-24 bytes            | 1.38x | 1.82x |
| `String`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | 2-10 bytes            | 5.42x | 9.07x |
| `String`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | sorted 8-24 bytes     | 3.57x | 4.54x |
| `String`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | 4-24 bytes, 10% nulls | 3.10x | 4.23x |
| `Binary`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | 4-24 bytes            | 4.03x | 4.46x |
| `List[String]`: PLAIN      | 2-10 bytes            | 1.07x | 1.13x |

### `head` vs `2.10.0`
_(all changes since the last release, eg: #30609, #30628, etc)_

|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| `String`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes            | 1.58x | 3.13x |

issue.title: Iceberg: read the metadata tables (snapshots, history, files, manifests)
issue.body:
### Description

I would like a Polars way to read the metadata tables of an Iceberg table (snapshots, history, files, manifests, partitions).

On `main` (`fd703335f7`), Polars' Iceberg API is `scan_iceberg`, `LazyFrame.sink_iceberg`, `DataFrame.write_iceberg` and `delete_iceberg`. None of them can read the metadata tables of an Iceberg table (snapshots, history, files, manifests, partitions), so a Polars pipeline has to call pyiceberg directly:

```python
import tempfile

import polars as pl
from pyiceberg.catalog.sql import SqlCatalog

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
cat = SqlCatalog("lake", uri=f"sqlite:///{d}/c.db", warehouse=f"file://{d}")
pl.LazyFrame({"id": [1, 2], "v": [10, 20]}).sink_iceberg(
    "sales.orders",
    catalog=cat,
    mode="append",
    create_if_not_exists=True,
    create_namespace_if_not_exists=True,
)
tbl = cat.load_table("sales.orders")
snapshots = pl.from_arrow(tbl.inspect.snapshots())
files = pl.from_arrow(tbl.inspect.files())
```

These are what you need to choose a `snapshot_id` for `scan_iceberg` or a range for its incremental scan. `pl.Catalog` has this kind of call (`create_table`, `delete_table`, `create_namespace`, `delete_namespace`, `list_tables`), but only for Unity Catalog (see #27394).

Context: we test what each engine can do on Iceberg (https://djouallah.github.io/lakehouse_benchmark/#features). "Metadata tables" is a row there; Spark, Sail, Trino, DuckDB, chDB and Databend support it. Checked on a Polars main build (`fd703335f7`), run: https://github.com/djouallah/lakehouse_benchmark/actions/runs/39779269923.

issue.title: Lazy `col.slice(1, 2).head(2)` applies the slice twice
issue.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]})
print(lf.select(pl.col("a").slice(1, 2).head(2)).collect()["a"].to_list())
# [3], expected [2, 3]
```

### Log output

With `scan_parquet` as the source, the plan shows both slices:

```shell
SELECT [col("a").slice(offset=1, length=2)]
  Parquet SCAN [x.parquet]
  PROJECT */1 COLUMNS
  SLICE: Positive { offset: 1, len: 2 }
```

### Issue description

When every column of a lazy `select` is sliced, the slice is moved below the `select`, but the expression slice stays, so the rows are sliced twice. It happens when an outer `head`/`limit`/`slice` doesn't shorten the inner slice (`slice(1, 2).head(5)` also gives `[3]`, `slice(1, 1).head(1)` gives `[]`), and a negative outer slice over an elementwise expression returns other rows: `pl.col("a").abs().slice(1).tail(2)` gives `[3, 4]` instead of `[4, 5]`. Next to a second sliced column (`b = a * 10`, `pl.col("b").slice(1, 2)`), the in-memory engine raises `ShapeError` and the streaming engine broadcasts the short column, giving rows that don't line up: `[(3, 20), (3, 30)]` instead of `[(2, 20), (3, 30)]`. Both engines are affected; the eager `df.select(...)` and `QueryOptFlags(slice_pushdown=False)` give the right answer.

This is the expression slice pushdown in `slice_pushdown_expr.rs`, like #30666. Polars 1.39.0 is right and 1.40.1 is wrong, which points at #27200.

### Expected behavior

`[2, 3]`.

### Installed versions

Reproduces on 2.0.0, 2.1.0 and main (236ce41367).

issue.title: Lazy `.first()`/`.head(n)` after `list.eval` or `list.reverse` cuts every list
issue.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"l": [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5]]})
print(lf.select(pl.col("l").list.eval(pl.element() + 1).first()).collect()["l"].to_list())
# [[2]]  expected [[2, 3, 4]]
```

### Log output

```shell
>>> lf.select(pl.col("l").list.eval(pl.element() + 1).first()).explain()
SELECT [col("l").list.eval(element().slice(offset=0, length=1) + 1).first()]
  DF ["l"]; PROJECT */1 COLUMNS
```

### Issue description

The row slice is pushed into the list evaluation, so it cuts each list instead of the rows. It happens with
`.first()`, `.last()`, `.head(n)`, `.tail(n)` and `.slice()` after `list.eval`, `list.agg`, `list.reverse`,
`arr.eval` and `struct.with_fields`, on both engines and inside `group_by().agg()`. The eager `df.select(...)`
and `QueryOptFlags(slice_pushdown=False)` give the right answer.

`aexpr_slice_pushdown_top` (`slice_pushdown_expr.rs`) takes push locations from all inputs of an elementwise
node, including the `evaluation` of `Eval`. Polars 1.39.0 is right and 1.40.1 is wrong, which points at #27200.

### Expected behavior

`[[2, 3, 4]]`, the first row with its whole list.

### Installed versions

Reproduces on 2.0.0, 2.1.0 and main (8dcc6b28e2).

issue.title: #28498 feeds fabricated nulls to user code, so a null-free query can fail
issue.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
import polars as pl


def strict(s: pl.Series) -> pl.Series:
    """An elementwise kernel that rejects null, proxy for a real plugin kernel."""
    if s.null_count():
        msg = f"null input is not supported, got {s.to_list()}"
        raise ValueError(msg)
    return s * 10


expr = pl.col("x").map_batches(strict, return_dtype=pl.Int64, is_elementwise=True)
df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3]})  # no nulls anywhere

print(f"polars {pl.__version__}")
try:
    print("  ", df.select(r=pl.when(pl.col("x") == 2).then(expr).otherwise(0)).to_series().to_list())
    raise SystemExit(0)
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"   {exc}")
    raise SystemExit(1) from None
```


### Log output

```shell
$ uv run --with "polars==1.43.2" t.py
polars 1.43.2
   [0, 20, 0]

$ uv run --with "polars==1.44.1" t.py
polars 1.44.1
   null input is not supported, got [None, 2, None]

This error occurred in the following expression:
        col("x").python_udf()
while evaluating this larger expression:
        .when([(col("x")) == (2)]).then(col("x").python_udf()).otherwise(0)
```

### Issue description

#28498 masks the irrelevant elements of an elementwise `when` arm to null before evaluating it.

For polars' own kernels that is sound, since they propagate null. For **opaque user code** it is not: `is_elementwise=True` promises row independence, not null tolerance, so polars cannot know the callee accepts a null it never received.

Two consequences, and the second one is silent:

1. A null-rejecting kernel fails on data with no nulls, as above.
2. A kernel whose result depends on the value stops seeing it. I hit this in an **expression plugin** of probability distributions: the plugin validates its parameters per row (raising `ComputeError` on an invalid parameterisation, returning null for a null parameter), and six methods call it inside a `when` arm. On 1.44.1 the invalid rows arrive as null, the null path takes over, and an invalid parameterisation is accepted silently.

### Expected behavior

Honestly, I am not sure what can be a solution here.

_Maybe_ skip the masking when the arm contains user code (`AnonymousFunction`, so `map_batches` and `register_plugin_function`), keeping the optimisation for native kernels. Passing only the *selected* rows would work for user code too, since row independence already licenses it; what user code cannot handle is an input value the caller never supplied.

df = pl.DataFrame({"ts": [5, 5, 5, 5], "v": [1, 9, 2, 8]})

issue.title: `join(maintain_order=...).head(n)` takes the wrong rows when a `sort`, `unique` or aggregation follows
issue.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
import polars as pl

left = pl.LazyFrame({"k": [1, 0]})
right = pl.LazyFrame({"k": [0, 1], "w": [1, 2]})
q = left.join(right, on="k", maintain_order="left").head(1)

print(q.collect(engine="in-memory")["w"].to_list())            # [2]
print(q.sort("w").collect(engine="in-memory")["w"].to_list())  # [1], expected [2]
```

### Log output

```shell
[2]
[1]
```

### Issue description

`head(n)` on its own is right, but with an order-insensitive step on top (`sort`, `unique`, `sum`) the query takes
`n` rows of the join in some other order. It happens with `head`, `tail` and `slice`, for inner, left, right, full
and cross joins and every `maintain_order` value. The streaming engine returns other rows on most runs; the in-memory
engine is wrong whenever its own output order differs from the requested one, as above. Eager,
`QueryOptFlags(slice_pushdown=False)` and `QueryOptFlags(check_order_observe=False)` give the right answer.

Slice pushdown moves the `head` into the join's own slice, and then the `IR::Join` arm of `simplify_ordering`
(`simplify_ordering/mod.rs:473`) drops `maintain_order` because nothing above observes the output order. The `Sort`,
`GroupBy` and `Distinct` arms skip this when they carry a slice (`options.slice.is_none()`); the `Join` arm doesn't.
#28419, #28448, #28551 and #28556 fixed the cases where the sliced join is the final output.

### Expected behavior

`[2]`, the same row `head(1)` returns.

### Installed versions

Reproduces on 2.0.0, 2.1.0 and main (8dcc6b28e2).

labels.name: repo-6716405b
labels.description: New feature or an improvement of an existing feature

issue.body:
When a query only references some fields of a struct column, `scan_parquet` still fetches and decodes **every** Parquet leaf column under that struct. Cost scales with the width of the struct, not with the fields the query uses.

```python
import polars as pl

# payload: Struct with 64 fields
pl.scan_parquet("nested.parquet").select(pl.col("payload").struct.field("f1")).collect()
```

This reads and decodes all 64 leaves of `payload`. Storing the same data unnested (`payload_f1`, `payload_f2`, …) only reads one column chunk per row group.

Wide structs are common in practice: event payloads, JSON-derived data, Spark/Delta exports, and shredded Variant columns. On object storage the extra column chunks also mean extra bytes over the network.

Row-group skipping on struct fields already works since #27887 (per-field struct statistics), so `filter(pl.col("s").struct.field("x") > 5)` prunes row groups. What is missing is the projection side: after skipping, all sibling leaves are still fetched and decoded.

### Benchmark

Same data in two layouts: `nested.parquet` (`id` plus one struct `payload` with F fields of mixed i64/f64/str) and `flat.parquet` (the same fields as top-level columns). Each query runs in its own process, `engine="streaming"`, median of 5 runs after 1 warmup.

Polars 2.1.0, Python 3.14.9, macOS (local SSD, files in page cache), 2,000,000 rows, 64 fields, row_group_size 100,000.

| query | flat (ms) | nested (ms) | nested / flat | peak RSS flat (MiB) | peak RSS nested (MiB) | row groups read (nested) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `one_field` | 2.3 | 201.7 | 87.7x | 138 | 1442 | n/a |
| `three_fields` | 5.8 | 201.5 | 34.6x | 252 | 1471 | n/a |
| `filter_1pct_one_field` | 2.1 | 83.5 | 39.5x | 90 | 363 | 1/20 |
| `full_struct` (baseline) | 115.5 | 197.8 | 1.7x | 2042 | 1741 | n/a |

| query | compressed bytes under `payload` (MiB) | bytes the query needs (MiB) |
|---|---:|---:|
| `one_field` | 318.2 | 6.1 |
| `three_fields` | 318.2 | 15.0 |
| `filter_1pct_one_field` | 318.2 | 8.0 |
| `full_struct` | 318.2 | 318.2 |

Takeaways:

- Selecting one field out of 64 is ~88x slower and uses ~10x the peak memory compared to the flat layout. The nested timing is the same (~200 ms) whether 1, 3 or all 64 fields are selected, so the cost is fully determined by the struct width.
- The query needs 6.1 MiB of compressed data but the reader fetches 318.2 MiB (~52x). Locally this is hidden by the page cache; on object storage it is real network traffic.
- Row-group skipping on a struct field works (1 of 20 row groups read), but the surviving row group is still decoded in full, so the filtered query remains ~40x slower than flat.

Benchmark script: [bench_struct_projection.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33936882/bench_struct_projection.py)

### Where this happens (main @ 7f902bd)

The streaming Parquet reader works on root column names throughout:

- `crates/polars-stream/src/nodes/io_sources/parquet/row_group_data_fetch.rs`, `get_row_group_byte_ranges_for_projection`: byte ranges come from `columns_under_root_iter(col_name)`, i.e. all leaves under the root.
- `crates/polars-stream/src/nodes/io_sources/parquet/row_group_decode.rs`, `decode_column` / `decode_column_prefiltered`: all leaves under the root are passed to `to_deserializer` together with the full `ArrowField`.
- `crates/polars-stream/src/nodes/io_sources/parquet/statistics.rs`, `load_parquet_column_statistics` / `load_struct_column_statistics`: struct statistics are built by matching arrow fields to `columns_idxs_under_root_iter` leaves by position and bail out if the leaf count does not match.
- The projection handed to the reader (`Projection` / `ArrowFieldProjection`) is a schema of root columns, built by projection pushdown in `polars-plan`.

### Proposed approach

1. **Planner.** In projection pushdown, collect the struct field paths that are actually referenced per root column. If the struct is ever used as a whole (`pl.col("s")`, `struct.with_fields`, `unnest`, a struct passed to a UDF, …), keep the full struct. Otherwise pass a **narrowed struct dtype** in the scan's projected schema (`s: Struct{x, y}` instead of the full struct). Expressing the pruning as a dtype keeps the scan interface unchanged. One catch: the multi-scan column selector (`multi_scan/components/column_selector/builder.rs`) checks file structs against the target dtype using `extra_struct_fields` / `missing_struct_fields`, and a narrowed target would trip the extra-fields check. The narrowing therefore has to be marked as a projection (prune the file field first, then cast), not treated as a user-specified target schema.
2. **Reader.** Prune the file's `ArrowField` to the requested children and select only the leaf column chunks whose `path_in_schema` matches, both when computing byte ranges and when decoding. Definition and repetition levels are per leaf, so decoding a struct with a subset of children should not need changes in the nested deserializer. This needs test coverage first.
3. **Statistics.** Build the per-field statistics from the same pruned field and leaf subset, so row-group skipping keeps working together with the pruned projection.
4. **Scope for a first version.** Structs, including nested structs. Structs inside lists/maps keep reading the full column for now.

Tests I would add: nested structs; struct containing Datetime/Date fields (cf. #29756); struct containing a list; multi-file and hive scans where files have different struct fields (`missing_struct_fields` / `extra_struct_fields`); `allow_missing_columns`; filter and projection on different fields of the same struct; and a check that the struct is read in full when it is used as a whole.

I am happy to work on a PR for this. Before I start: does this direction (narrowed struct dtype in the scan projection) fit how you want the scan pipeline to evolve, or would you prefer a different representation for nested projections?

issue.body:
### Description

For struct columns, sometimes only a subset of the fields are observed in the output of the query. These fields can potentially be dropped much earlier in the query than what we currently do. As an example -

```python
import polars as pl


def raise_exc():
    raise Exception()


q = (
    pl.LazyFrame({"a": 1})
    .with_columns(
        b=pl.col("a").map_elements(lambda _: raise_exc(), return_dtype=pl.Int64)
    )
    .select("a")
)

print(q.collect())
# shape: (1, 1)
# ┌─────┐
# │ a   │
# │ --- │
# │ i64 │
# ╞═════╡
# │ 1   │
# └─────┘

q = (
    pl.LazyFrame({"a": 1})
    .with_columns(
        b=pl.struct(
            (
                pl.col("a")
                .map_elements(lambda _: raise_exc(), return_dtype=pl.Int64)
                .alias("field_a")
            ),
            pl.lit(1, dtype=pl.Int64).alias("field_b"),
        )
    )
    .select("a", pl.col("b").struct.field("field_b"))
)

print(q.collect())
# Exception

```

For the 2nd example, we should be able to skip evaluating the `map_elements()` expression entirely, allowing the query to succeed with the following output:
```python
shape: (1, 2)
┌─────┬─────────┐
│ a   ┆ field_b │
│ --- ┆ ---     │
│ i64 ┆ i64     │
╞═════╪═════════╡
│ 1   ┆ 1       │
└─────┴─────────┘
```

Once this is in place, we can potentially skip reading struct field columns that are unused when scanning from e.g. Parquet.

issue.title: Join reordering joins two in-memory tables on a non-unique key first (6x peak memory)
issue.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://crates.io/crates/polars) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
import inspect, resource, subprocess, sys
import polars as pl

T, F, N = 8760, 255, 30  # time steps, flows, nodes
time = pl.DataFrame({"t": range(T)})
flows = pl.DataFrame({"f": range(F)})
var = flows.join(time, how="cross").with_row_index("col_id").lazy()  # unique on (f, t): 2.2M rows
fmap = flows.with_columns(n=pl.col("f") % N).lazy()                   # unique on f: 255 rows
rows = pl.DataFrame({"n": range(N)}).join(time, how="cross").with_row_index("rid").lazy()  # unique on (n, t): 263k rows

# two many-to-one joins: no intermediate is larger than var
q = rows.join(var.join(fmap, on="f"), on=["t", "n"]).select("rid", "col_id")

HAS_FLAG = "join_order" in inspect.signature(pl.QueryOptFlags).parameters  # polars >= 2
opt = lambda on: {"optimizations": pl.QueryOptFlags(join_order=on)} if HAS_FLAG else {}

if len(sys.argv) == 1:
    print(pl.__version__)
    for on in (True, False):
        print(f"--- explain(join_order={on})\n{q.explain(**opt(on))}")
    for on in ("True", "False"):
        subprocess.run([sys.executable, __file__, on])
else:
    n = q.collect(**opt(sys.argv[1] == "True")).height
    rss = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss // 1024  # KiB on Linux
    print(f"join_order={sys.argv[1]:5s} rows={n:,} peak RSS {rss:,} MB", flush=True)
```

Output on 2.1.0:

```
2.1.0
--- explain(join_order=True)
simple π 2/2 ["rid", "col_id"]
  INNER JOIN:
  LEFT PLAN ON: [col("f"), col("n")]
    simple π 4/4 ["rid", "col_id", "f", "n"]
      INNER JOIN:
      BUILD SIDE: PreferLeft
      LEFT PLAN ON: [col("t")]
        DF ["rid", "n", "t"]; PROJECT */3 COLUMNS
      RIGHT PLAN ON: [col("t")]
        DF ["col_id", "f", "t"]; PROJECT */3 COLUMNS
      END INNER JOIN
  RIGHT PLAN ON: [col("f"), col("n")]
    DF ["f", "n"]; PROJECT */2 COLUMNS
  END INNER JOIN
--- explain(join_order=False)
simple π 2/2 ["rid", "col_id"]
  INNER JOIN:
  LEFT PLAN ON: [col("t"), col("n")]
    DF ["rid", "n", "t"]; PROJECT */3 COLUMNS
  RIGHT PLAN ON: [col("t"), col("n")]
    simple π 3/3 ["col_id", "t", "n"]
      INNER JOIN:
      BUILD SIDE: PreferRight
      LEFT PLAN ON: [col("f")]
        DF ["col_id", "f", "t"]; PROJECT */3 COLUMNS
      RIGHT PLAN ON: [col("f")]
        DF ["f", "n"]; PROJECT */2 COLUMNS
      END INNER JOIN
  END INNER JOIN
join_order=True  rows=2,233,800 peak RSS 1,873 MB
join_order=False rows=2,233,800 peak RSS 312 MB
```

On 1.44.2 (no `join_order` flag, joins run as written) both runs peak at about 372 MB.

### Log output

```shell
`POLARS_VERBOSE=1`, `join_order=True` (graph-state lines omitted):


choosing build side, sample lengths are: 262800 vs. 2233800
build side chosen: left
choosing build side, sample lengths are: 67014000 vs. 255
build side chosen: right
join_order=True  rows=2,233,800 peak RSS 1,874 MB
```

### Issue description

With join reordering, `rows.join(var, on="t")` runs first. `t` repeats on both sides (30 rows per `t` in `rows`, 255 in `var`), so it yields 67M rows before the `(f, n)` join with `fmap` cuts it back to 2.2M. Peak RSS goes from 0.3 GB to 1.9 GB here; in our application (String keys, more columns) the process peak went from 8 GB on 1.44.2 to 25 GB on 2.1.0. `join_order=False` restores it with identical results; `row_estimate=False` and the streaming engine do not help.

**Likely cause** (from reading `optimizer/join_order`): in-memory frames carry only row counts, so for a key without statistics the smaller side is guessed unique. `rows` is guessed unique on `t`, although only `(n, t)` is unique, so `rows.join(var, on="t")` is estimated at 2.2M rows instead of 67M (about 30× under). #30191's rule does not fire, because it only drops a guess when a leaf has several, and `rows` has just one (towards `fmap` it is the larger side). All three start orders then cost the same, and the tie goes to the first leaf in written order, `rows`.

So the plan depends on how the query is written. Writing `var` or `fmap` first gives the good plan:

| written as | first join |
|---|---|
| `rows.join(var.join(fmap, on="f"), on=["t", "n"])` | on `t` (bad) |
| `rows.join(fmap, on="n").join(var, on=["f", "t"])` | on `t` (bad) |
| `var.join(fmap, on="f").join(rows, on=["t", "n"])` | on `f` (good) |
| `fmap.join(var, on="f").join(rows, on=["t", "n"])` | on `f` (good) |

The shape of #30191's own test (fact / dim / price) does the same on 2.1.0 when it uses in-memory frames and is written price-first (that test uses parquet with an integer `ts`, which has a range and so is not guessed):

```python
fact = pl.LazyFrame({"ts": [t for t in range(40) for _ in range(100)], "duid": [f"U{u}" for u in range(100)] * 40})
dim = pl.LazyFrame({"duid": [f"U{u}" for u in range(100)], "region": [f"R{u % 5}" for u in range(100)]})
price = pl.LazyFrame({"ts": [t for t in range(40) for _ in range(5)], "region": [f"R{r}" for r in range(5)] * 40})
print(price.join(fact.join(dim, on="duid"), on=["ts", "region"]).explain())  # first join: price with fact on ts
```

One possible fix: when a leaf joins a larger leaf on one key and a smaller leaf on another, and those two also join each other, guess it unique only on both keys together (as #30191's comment says, "price has one row per (ts, region)"). I have a candidate patch with tests if that is useful.

In general, it could be useful to be able to declare unique keys, but that goes beyond this bug report.

### Expected behavior

The reordered plan should not create a larger intermediate than the written order: here `var.join(fmap, on="f")` first, then the join with `rows` on `(t, n)`, as `join_order=False` and 1.44.2 do, whatever order the query is written in.

### Installed versions

```

Polars:              2.1.0
Build:               7f902bd3ffd27ff82d14278a09a295ff2f7aed92
Index type:          UInt32
Platform:            Linux-6.14.0-37-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.39
Python:              3.12.3 (main, Aug 31 2026, 10:18:26) [GCC 13.3.0]
Runtime:             rt32
```

(Optional dependencies omitted; none involved. Comparison: polars 1.44.2, same machine and Python.)

import resource
import polars as pl

    pl.DataFrame({"day": pl.int_range(n_day, eager=True)})

    skel.lazy()

    chain()
    .group_by(pl.col("ent").alias("id"), "ts", "day")

    .rename({"id": "ent"})
)
q = chain().select("id", "ts", "day", "ent").join(per, on=["ent", "ts", "day"])

flags = pl.QueryOptFlags(join_order=True)

issue.title: perf: Optimise decoding of Parquet `String` and `Binary` columns
issue.body:
Following on from the nested dtype optimisations in #30601, more profiling of flat/scalar Parquet reads showed decoding overhead for `String` and `Binary`, _especially_ for the `DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY` encoding[^1].

**Spoiler:** `DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY` encoding goes from ~5x slower than `pyarrow` to 1.1 → 2x faster. 🎉

# Changes

Both delta decoders were moved out of the `BinViewDecoder` match arms into a new `binview/delta.rs` module to consolidate/clarify, and `delta_byte_array::Decoder` drops the now-unused per-value iterator (dead code).

* **`PLAIN`**: short values (≤12 bytes, stored inline in the view) are now cut from a 16-byte block of the page instead of being copied one at a time.

* **`DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY`**: each page is decoded into views in bulk (all lengths at once,  one buffer, one UTF8 check per page); nulls and filters then reuse the existing PLAIN primitive kernels.

* ⭐ **`DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY`**: was allocating three `Vecs` per value and decoding the prefix/suffix lengths one at a time. Lengths are now decoded in bulk, and values are rebuilt in a single scratch buffer with fixed-size block copies.

**Also:**
* Delta-encoded pages with corrupt lengths now raise a `ComputeError` instead of panicking.
* Streamlined the `new_inline_from_block` function.

# Speedups 🚀

Testing on 20M rows[^2], `pyarrow`-written parquet, release build, single-column reads vs `main`.
Measured end-to-end with zstd (default threads) and uncompressed (single thread)[^3]:

_(all changes since the last release, eg: #30609, #30628, etc)_

|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| `String`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes            | 1.58x | 3.13x |

|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|

@alexander-beedie One memory regression still for nested/slice heads:

```
One remaining finding on 7e0c0fc2e6:

[P2] Handle shortened and empty masks as partial selections — [delta.rs:58](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/7e0c0fc2e62c5fd4effceac6eddd671cfa69d37e/crates/polars-parquet/src/arrow/read/deserialize/binview/delta.rs#L58)

Reproduced reading one row from delta-encoded lists containing repeated 64 KiB strings:

- Single page: 76 MiB, versus 12 MiB on the exact base.
- Multiple pages: 270 MiB, versus 14 MiB on base.

Derive the selection bounds even for all-true masks; an empty mask must select zero values.
```

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
import time

import polars as pl
from polars.testing import assert_frame_equal


def left_join_where_workaround(lf_left, lf_right, left_on, right_on, predicate):
    # Hash join on the equality key, filter, then left join back on a row index so
    # unmatched left rows appear exactly once.
    lf_left = lf_left.with_row_index("_idx")
    lf_matches = (
        lf_left.join(lf_right, left_on=left_on, right_on=right_on, how="inner", coalesce=False)
        .filter(predicate)
        .select("_idx", *lf_right.collect_schema().names())
    )
    return lf_left.join(lf_matches, on="_idx", how="left").drop("_idx")


def make_data(n):
    def col(high, seed):
        return pl.int_range(high, eager=True).sample(n, with_replacement=True, seed=seed)

    lf_left = pl.LazyFrame({"id_x": col(n // 10, 0), "val_x": col(100, 1)})
    lf_right = pl.LazyFrame({"id_y": col(n // 10, 2), "val_y": col(100, 3)})
    return lf_left, lf_right


predicate = pl.col("val_x") <= pl.col("val_y")

lf_left, lf_right = make_data(n=1_000)
print(lf_left.join_where(lf_right, pl.col("id_x") == pl.col("id_y"), predicate, how="left").explain())

for n in [10_000, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000]:
    lf_left, lf_right = make_data(n=n)

    start = time.perf_counter()
    df_join_where = lf_left.join_where(
        lf_right, pl.col("id_x") == pl.col("id_y"), predicate, how="left"
    ).collect()
    t_join_where = time.perf_counter() - start

    start = time.perf_counter()
    df_workaround = left_join_where_workaround(
        lf_left, lf_right, left_on="id_x", right_on="id_y", predicate=predicate
    ).collect()
    t_workaround = time.perf_counter() - start

    assert_frame_equal(df_join_where, df_workaround, check_row_order=False)
    print(f"n={n:>6}: join_where {t_join_where:7.3f}s, workaround {t_workaround:.3f}s")
```

### Log output

```shell
LEFT NESTED LOOP JOIN ON (col("id_x") == col("id_y")) & (col("val_x") <= col("val_y")):
LEFT PLAN:
  DF ["id_x", "val_x"]; PROJECT */2 COLUMNS
RIGHT PLAN:
  DF ["id_y", "val_y"]; PROJECT */2 COLUMNS
END LEFT NESTED LOOP JOIN
n= 10000: join_where   0.022s, workaround 0.005s
n= 20000: join_where   0.052s, workaround 0.002s
n= 40000: join_where   3.207s, workaround 0.003s
n= 80000: join_where  17.886s, workaround 0.004s
```

### Issue description

`join_where(how="left")` with an equality predicate plus a predicate referencing both tables is planned as a `LEFT NESTED LOOP JOIN`, so runtime grows quadratically with the input size. The same happens for `pl.col("id_x").eq_missing(pl.col("id_y"))`, for `is_between` conditions, and even when the only other predicate is `pl.lit(True)`.

An equivalent implementation using the existing hash join (inner join on the equality key → filter → left join back on a row index) produces identical results (asserted above) and is ~4000x faster at 80k rows.

This follows up on #29119, which was closed because the comparison there wasn't equivalent (it duplicated unmatched left rows). The workaround above handles that case correctly, which shows the slowdown isn't inherent to left-join semantics.

### Expected behavior

When the predicates contain at least one equality between left and right columns, `join_where(how="left")` should use the hash join on the equality keys and apply the remaining predicates on the candidate pairs, with performance comparable to the workaround above. This is the approach suggested by @ritchie46 in #18669 ("Choose the equality predicates as outer join and add the remaining as filters").

issue.title: Join reordering can greatly reduce performance
issue.body:
Reproducer:
```python
import time
import resource
import polars as pl


n_ent, n_day = 500, 100
ent = pl.int_range(n_ent, eager=True)
skel = (
    pl.DataFrame({"day": pl.int_range(n_day, eager=True)})
    .with_columns(ts=pl.col("day"))
    .join(pl.DataFrame({"id": ent}), how="cross")
)
id_map = pl.DataFrame({"id": ent, "tk": ent, "known_from": 0, "valid_from": 0})
ents = pl.DataFrame({"ent": ent, "tk": ent})
chain = lambda: (
    skel.lazy()
    .join(id_map.lazy(), on="id")
    .filter(pl.col("known_from") <= pl.col("ts"))
    .filter(pl.col("valid_from") <= pl.col("day"))
    .join(ents.lazy(), on="tk")
)
per = (
    chain()
    .group_by(pl.col("ent").alias("id"), "ts", "day")
    .agg(v=pl.len())
    .rename({"id": "ent"})
)
q = chain().select("id", "ts", "day", "ent").join(per, on=["ent", "ts", "day"])

flags = pl.QueryOptFlags(join_order=True)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
_ = q.collect(optimizations=flags)
t1 = time.perf_counter()
time_taken = (t1 - t0) * 1000

max_rss = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss / 1024

print(f"Took {time_taken:.1f} ms")
print(f"Peak RSS: {max_rss:.1f} MB")
```

On Polars 2.1.0, this outputs on my machine:
```
Took 145.5 ms

```
If I disable `join_reorder`, or use Polars < 2.0.0, I get something like:
```

```

This looks related to #30647

issue.title: perf: Optimise decoding of Parquet `String` and `Binary` columns
issue.body:
Following on from the nested dtype optimisations in #30601, more profiling of flat/scalar Parquet reads showed decoding overhead for `String` and `Binary`, _especially_ for the `DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY` encoding[^1].

**Spoiler:** `DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY` encoding goes from ~5x slower than `pyarrow` to 1.1 → 2x faster. 🎉

# Changes

Both delta decoders were moved out of the `BinViewDecoder` match arms into a new `binview/delta.rs` module to consolidate/clarify, and `delta_byte_array::Decoder` drops the now-unused per-value iterator (dead code).

* **`PLAIN`**: short values (≤12 bytes, stored inline in the view) are now cut from a 16-byte block of the page instead of being copied one at a time.

* **`DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY`**: each page is decoded into views in bulk (all lengths at once,  one buffer, one UTF8 check per page); nulls and filters then reuse the existing PLAIN primitive kernels.

* ⭐ **`DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY`**: was allocating three `Vecs` per value and decoding the prefix/suffix lengths one at a time. Lengths are now decoded in bulk, and values are rebuilt in a single scratch buffer with fixed-size block copies.

**Also:**
* Delta-encoded pages with corrupt lengths now raise a `ComputeError` instead of panicking.
* Streamlined the `new_inline_from_block` function.

# Speedups 🚀

Testing on 20M rows[^2], `pyarrow`-written parquet, release build, single-column reads vs `main`.
Measured end-to-end with zstd (default threads) and uncompressed (single thread)[^3]:

### This PR vs `main`

| type/encoding | data | zstd | uncompressed |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| `String`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes            | 1.11x | 1.44x |
| `String`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes, 10% nulls | 1.14x | 1.47x |
| `Binary`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes            | 1.11x | 1.49x |
| `String`: DELTA_LENGTH     | 2-10 bytes            | 1.37x | 1.86x |
| `String`: DELTA_LENGTH     | 4-24 bytes            | 1.38x | 1.82x |
| `String`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | 2-10 bytes            | 5.42x | 9.07x |
| `String`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | sorted 8-24 bytes     | 3.57x | 4.54x |
| `String`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | 4-24 bytes, 10% nulls | 3.10x | 4.23x |
| `Binary`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | 4-24 bytes            | 4.03x | 4.46x |
| `List[String]`: PLAIN      | 2-10 bytes            | 1.07x | 1.13x |

### `head` vs `2.10.0`
_(all changes since the last release, eg: #30609, #30628, etc)_

| type/encoding | data | zstd | uncompressed |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| `String`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes            | 1.58x | 3.13x |
| `String`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes, 10% nulls | 1.59x | 2.71x |
| `Binary`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes            | 1.56x | 3.39x |
| `String`: DELTA_LENGTH     | 2-10 bytes            | 1.80x | 2.87x |

| `List[String]`: PLAIN      | 2-10 bytes            | 1.58x | 2.11x |

### `polars` vs `pyarrow`

| type/encoding | data | 2.1.0 (zstd) | now (zstd) | 2.1.0 (uncompressed) | now (uncompressed) |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `String`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes            | 4.7× faster | 7.5× faster | 1.1× faster     | 3.5× faster |
| `String`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes, 10% nulls | 4.7× faster | 7.4× faster | 1.1× faster     | 2.9× faster |
| `Binary`: PLAIN            | 2-10 bytes            | 4.7× faster | 7.3× faster | 1.2× faster     | 4.0× faster |
| `String`: DELTA_LENGTH     | 2-10 bytes            | 4.2× faster | 7.5× faster | ⬇ 1.1× slower     | ⬆ 2.7× faster |

| `String`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | 2-10 bytes            | 1.2× faster | 6.9× faster | ⬇ **4.9× slower** | ⬆ 2.0× faster |
| `String`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | sorted 8-24 bytes     | 1.9× faster | 7.0× faster | ⬇ **2.6× slower** | ⬆ 1.8× faster |
| `String`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | 4-24 bytes, 10% nulls | 1.5× faster | 4.8× faster | ⬇ **4.0× slower** | ⬆ 1.1× faster |
| `Binary`: DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY | 4-24 bytes            | **≈ on par**      | 4.2× faster | ⬇ **4.4× slower** | ⬆ 1.1× faster |

**AI 🤖:** Profiling, prototyping and the initial implementation were done in conjunction with Opus 5.5. Final version is a mix of human (me) and AI.

comment.body:
Courtesy of astra:

```
Two findings on 125c548e1a:

1. [P2] Apply filtering before retaining decoded payloads — [delta.rs:166–167](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/125c548e1a0bd51bc3cd80179db28cf8e74a141c/crates/polars-parquet/src/arrow/read/deserialize/binview/delta.rs#L166-L167)
   Every non-inline value is copied before applying the filter. With PyArrow’s default page sizing, a 66 KB file containing 1,024 identical 64 KiB strings now peaks at 76 MiB versus 12 MiB on base when reading just one row. Larger pages and sparse filters can cause substantial memory growth or OOM. Preserve prefix reconstruction in scratch, but retain only selected values and stop at the filter’s end.
2. [P2] Preserve native field layout in the new inline path — [mod.rs:349](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/125c548e1a0bd51bc3cd80179db28cf8e74a141c/crates/polars-parquet/src/arrow/read/deserialize/binview/mod.rs#L349)
   The newly used block constructor packs a little-endian integer, then transmutes it into native-endian View fields. On big-endian targets, "abc" becomes a view with length zero; 12-byte values can become invalid non-inline references. The previous constructor preserved native field layout. Use an endian-correct construction or fall back to View::new_inline on big-endian targets.

Validation: 200 crate tests passed, plus 672 PLAIN-versus-delta comparisons covering nulls, nested lists, slices, and masks. Memory regression reproduced against base; endian finding is from code inspection
```

issue.title: perf: Speed up inline binary view construction for short strings
issue.body:
Builds on #30609; speeds It up a bit (branchless now) while also removing the "unsafe" `transmute`✌️ 

Am working on some other speedups in this area and there was crossover :)

## Changes

* `View::new_inline_unchecked` branched on `len >= 8` to choose its loads, which mispredicts when lengths vary around 8 bytes (as short strings are often likely to do). Values of 4-12 bytes now share one path, with the choice made by selects instead.

* Drops `unsafe` _(slice loads instead of raw pointer reads, fields instead of transmute)._

## Speedups 🚀

Test data - all short strings between 2 and 12 bytes.

issue.title: fix: Geoparquet fixes and features
issue.body:
Extended the geoparquet reading/writing to also support (covering) bounding boxes, which are part of the geoparquet and geoarrow spec, but need some conversion.
All new funcionality is locked behind the `POLARS_GEOPARQUET_WRITE` and `POLARS_GEOPARQUET_READ` envvars, just like the existing mechanism.
This does not have any domain-specific implementation other than some constants defined by the geoparquet standard.

Also contains various minor fixes to the geoparquet metadata handling so that GeoPolars can use the built-in parquet reader better.
I put them all in a single PR because they're all pretty small and it would probably unnecessarily cost more time to open up a separate PR for all of them. Let me know if you'd still prefer them in separate PRs though.

Fix 1: A null `crs` key in geoparquet means it is "OGC:CRS84", while in geoarrow a null key would imply no CRS. This correctly converts between the two during reading/writing.

Fix 2:
A geo key you pass through metadata= now takes priority, and Polars no longer tries to derive one. Before, the derivation ran first and raised on a string CRS such as "EPSG:4326" even when you'd supplied a correct key. With this change, metadata=gpl.geoparquet_metadata(df) works with POLARS_GEOPARQUET_WRITE set.
This does result in one small behaviour change, when you pass your own geo key.
In such a case, Polars no longer reads POLARS_GEOPARQUET_WRITE. This would allow a user to set a (for now) invalid value such as `2.0`, which would go unreported.
This would still be in-line with how polars handles metadata generally though, as the geoparquet is more of an exception case anyway.

Fix 3:
When the schema has GeoParquet metadata Polars can't/doesn't allow to write (such as a string CRS), the sink now raises before any file is opened. Before, it failed only after all the data had been written.

(minor) change in addition to all these: made the error message for giving a string value for a CRS (instead of projjson, which is what geoparquet requires) clearer, showing the user what to do if they run into this error.

issue.title: Comparison with a literal on the left returns one row when the right column was made from a literal
issue.body:
### Reproducible example

```python
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"p": [1, 2, 3]}).with_columns(x=pl.lit(5.0))

df.with_columns(y=pl.col("x") > pl.lit(0.0))  # height 3
df.with_columns(y=pl.lit(0.0) + pl.col("x"))  # height 3
df.with_columns(y=pl.lit(0.0) < pl.col("x"))  # raises
```

### Log output

```
polars.exceptions.InvalidOperationError: Series y, length 1 doesn't match the DataFrame height of 3

If you want expression: [(0.0) < (col("x"))] to be broadcasted, ensure it is a scalar (for instance by adding '.first()').
```

### Issue description

A comparison with a literal on the left and, on the right, a column made from a literal returns one row instead of the frame's height.

The column only has to have been made from a literal. Rebuilding the same values from a list makes the same comparison work:

```python
pl.DataFrame({"p": [1, 2, 3], "x": [5.0, 5.0, 5.0]}).with_columns(y=pl.lit(0.0) < pl.col("x"))  # height 3
```

What I tried, on the frame above:

| Expression | Result |
|---|---|
| `pl.lit(0.0) < pl.col("x")` | raises |
| `pl.lit(5.0) == pl.col("x")` | raises |
| `(pl.lit(1.0) + pl.lit(2.0)) < pl.col("x")` | raises |
| `pl.col("x") > pl.lit(0.0)` | height 3 |
| `pl.lit(0.0) + pl.col("x")` | height 3 |
| `pl.lit(0.0) < pl.col("p")` | height 3 |

- The lazy form fails the same way in the in-memory engine, with `optimizations=pl.QueryOptFlags.none()` as well. `engine="streaming"` gives height 3.
- `select("p", y=pl.lit(0.0) < pl.col("x"))` raises a `ShapeError` with the same message.
- It depends on the data when the column comes from a `when`, because of which rows take the literal branch:

```python
lf = pl.LazyFrame({"p": [1, 2, 3]})
for cut in (2, 0):
    x = pl.when(pl.col("p") > cut).then(pl.lit(5.0)).otherwise(pl.col("p").cast(pl.Float64))
    lf.with_columns(x=x).with_columns(y=pl.lit(0.0) < pl.col("x")).collect(engine="in-memory")
# cut=2 works; cut=0 raises, because every row takes the literal branch
```

So a query can work on one batch and raise on another.

A plain Python number on the left works, as `0.0 < pl.col("x")` reaches polars as `pl.col("x") > 0.0`. Swapping the operands is the workaround we use.

### Expected behavior

`y` has the frame's height, the same as `pl.col("x") > pl.lit(0.0)`: `[True, True, True]`.

### Installed versions

```
Polars:              2.1.0
Build:               7f902bd3ffd27ff82d14278a09a295ff2f7aed92
Index type:          UInt32
Platform:            Linux-5.15.133.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.39
Python:              3.13.15
Runtime:             rt32
```

Also reproduced on 2.0.0.

issue.title: Row-oriented DataFrame construction stores integers other than 1 as `false` in a Boolean column
issue.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame([[1], [2], [0], [3]], schema={"b": pl.Boolean}, orient="row", strict=False)
print(df["b"].to_list())
# [True, False, False, False]

print(pl.DataFrame({"b": [1, 2, 0, 3]}, schema={"b": pl.Boolean}, strict=False)["b"].to_list())
# [True, True, False, True]
print(pl.Series([1, 2, 0, 3]).cast(pl.Boolean).to_list())
# [True, True, False, True]
```

### Log output

```shell
No error or warning is raised.
```

### Issue description

When a DataFrame is built from rows (`orient="row"` or a list of dicts), an integer in a Boolean
column becomes `true` only if it is 1. Other values from 2 to 255 become `false`, and values outside
0 to 255 raise `ComputeError: could not append value`. The column-oriented constructor and `cast`
map every non-zero integer to `true`. With the default `strict=True` the row constructor also
returns `[True, False, False, False]` instead of raising; that part is #17375.

Possible cause: the Boolean arm of `AnyValueBuffer::add` extracts a `u8` and appends `v == 1`
([av_buffer.rs#L60-L63](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/ee5f3e7b6d4e47365094754fe7e3def51bce74d4/crates/polars-core/src/frame/row/av_buffer.rs#L60-L63)).

AI disclosure: the bug was found by a testing pipeline built with Claude Code, which also drafted
the reproducer. I ran the reproducer myself and wrote this report.

### Expected behavior

`[True, True, False, True]`, as from the column-oriented constructor. The `DataFrame` docstring for
`strict`: "If set to `False`, values that do not match the data type are cast to that data type or,
if casting is not possible, set to null instead." The
[casting guide](https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/expressions/casting/#booleans): "When converting
numbers to Booleans, the number 0 is converted to `False` and all other numbers are converted to
`True`".

issue.title: SQL: DELETE FROM an Iceberg table
issue.body:
### Description

I would like `DELETE FROM ... WHERE ...` in Polars SQL to delete the rows in an Iceberg table and commit.

Today `DELETE` only returns a filtered frame. Nothing is written to the table.

```python
ctx = pl.SQLContext()
# with a catalog attached (see #27776):
ctx.execute("DELETE FROM onelake.sales.orders WHERE id = 1")
```

Expected: one commit to the Iceberg table (delete files, or rewritten data files), and other engines no longer see the row.

Related: #27776 (attach an Iceberg REST catalog), #29843 (delete rows by predicate, DataFrame API).

Context: we test what each engine can do on Iceberg (https://djouallah.github.io/lakehouse_benchmark/#features). DELETE is part of the minimum to be usable. Spark, DuckDB, Sail and chDB support it in SQL.

issue.title: Base class for `pl.InProcessQuery` and `pc.DirectQuery` et. al.
issue.body: Polars cloud is bringing a lot of new concepts into polars, like planning engines / scaling modes, remote engines (which are defined in terms of an engine too, which is somewhat confusing), remote queries, etc. For queries in progress. I.e. `DirectQuery` or `ProxyQuery`, there was already a similar concept in bare `polars`: `InProcessQuery`. It would be good to unify those in terms of a base class, just like `QueryResult` has been unified. And it would also be good to consider whether these need to be generic (see #45, for example).

issue.title: Expose the observatory URI from a `ClusterContext`.
issue.body: You cannot access the observatory tied to a `ClusterContext` because its URI is buried in the connection's `SchedulerClient` Rust struct which does not expose it as a public attribute.

issue.title: Observatory: show the last IO source along with the first.
issue.body: It would be good for the plans displayed in the observatory to show the first and last source, and not just the first, of every `scan` operator. Since the filenames usually give information about the data queried and are sorted, this gives a way for the user to know the range scanned.

issue.title: Parity gap: SQL TRUNCATE on an Iceberg catalog table
issue.body:
### Description

Polars SQL can't run `TRUNCATE TABLE sales.orders` on a table of an attached Iceberg catalog, although the Python API can already do the same thing with `pl.delete_iceberg(tbl, pl.lit(True))`.

```python
import tempfile

import polars as pl
from pyiceberg.catalog.sql import SqlCatalog

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
cat = SqlCatalog("lake", uri=f"sqlite:///{d}/c.db", warehouse=f"file://{d}")
pl.LazyFrame({"id": [1, 2], "v": [10, 20]}).sink_iceberg(
    "sales.orders",
    catalog=cat,
    mode="append",
    create_if_not_exists=True,
    create_namespace_if_not_exists=True,
)
tbl = cat.load_table("sales.orders")

ctx = pl.SQLContext().register_catalog("lake", cat, default=True)
ctx.execute("""TRUNCATE TABLE sales.orders""", eager=True)
```

```
SQLInterfaceError: TRUNCATE on a table of attached catalog 'lake' is not supported
```

Expected: the statement commits to the Iceberg table, as `pl.delete_iceberg(tbl, pl.lit(True))` does.

Related: #29894 (DELETE FROM), #30113.

Context: we test what each engine can do on Iceberg (https://djouallah.github.io/lakehouse_benchmark/#features). "TRUNCATE" is a row there; Spark and Trino support it. Checked on a Polars main build (`fd703335f7`), run: https://github.com/djouallah/lakehouse_benchmark/actions/runs/39779269923.
